title: How to Choose a Senior Care Home in Memphis: The Four Things That Decide It
description: Care needs, memory, money and fit decide which Memphis-area senior care home works for a parent. How to judge each one, in order, before you tour anywhere.

main_html:
Quick answer

Choosing a senior care home in the Memphis area comes down to four things, and the order matters: care needs, memory, money and fit. Settle the first three on paper before you tour anywhere. Fit is the last filter, not the first.

A senior care home is the everyday name for a residence where an older adult lives and gets help with daily life. In Tennessee the licensed versions are the Assisted Care Living Facility, which helps with bathing, dressing, meals and medications, and its secured memory care unit for people living with dementia.

Families who start with fit, meaning the dining room, the paint, the friendliness of the person giving the tour, tend to fall for a community that cannot actually meet their parent's needs, or that the family cannot afford past the first year. Families who start with care needs end up with a short list that works, and then pick the one that feels right.

1. Care needs: what help does your parent need today?

Every licensed community in Shelby County will ask the same question before it agrees to take your parent: what help do they need, and how much of it? You can answer that before anyone asks.

Write down, honestly, what happens on an ordinary day. Professionals talk about activities of daily living: bathing, dressing, eating, using the toilet, moving from bed to chair, and continence. Alongside those sit the tasks that keep a household running: managing medications, cooking, shopping, handling money, using the phone, getting to appointments.

  • Help with one or two daily activities, and medication reminders: this is the core of assisted living.
  • Help with most daily activities, or two staff to move safely: some assisted living communities can do this at a higher care level; others will say no. Ask directly.
  • Daily skilled nursing such as wound care that needs a nurse every day, IV medicines, or a ventilator: this is usually a nursing home, not assisted living.
  • Short-term rehab after a hospital stay: a skilled nursing facility first, then assisted living or home.

Be specific when you write it down. "Mum needs some help" tells a community nothing. "Mum needs help getting in and out of the shower, cannot manage her pills, and has fallen twice since March" tells them exactly what care level to quote and whether they can meet it.

Ask your parent's doctor for a recent list of diagnoses and medications. Every community will need it, and the doctor's view of what is coming next, such as a progressive condition, is part of the care-needs picture. Our guide to activities of daily living and care levels walks through how communities score this and why it sets the price.

2. Memory: does your parent need a secured unit?

The second question splits the market in two. Of the 31 Assisted Care Living Facilities the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission licenses in Shelby County, 23 report secured beds, which is the state's term for memory care. The other eight do not have a secured unit at all.

The test is not the diagnosis. Plenty of people with early Alzheimer's live well in ordinary assisted living. The test is safety:

  • Does your parent wander, or try to leave home at night?
  • Have they got lost driving or walking somewhere familiar?
  • Do they forget they have eaten, or leave the stove on?
  • Do they become distressed or aggressive in ways that put themselves or others at risk?
  • Can they be left alone for an afternoon?

If the honest answer to any of the first four is yes, or to the last is no, put memory care on the list from the start. Moving into ordinary assisted living and then being asked to move again into the secured unit, often within months, is one of the hardest things a family can put a parent with dementia through.

Watch for the phrase "memory support". Some communities use it for a programme of activities inside ordinary assisted living, with no secured unit behind it. That is not the same thing. Our guide to memory care and when it is time explains the difference and what a secured unit should look like.

3. Money: what can the family pay, and for how long?

Assisted living is mostly paid privately, month by month, for as long as your parent lives there. CareScout's 2025 survey put the annual median cost of assisted living in Tennessee at $67,140, against $74,400 nationally. Memory care, higher care levels and a larger apartment all push the monthly bill above the median.

The question is not only "can we afford the first month?" It is "how many years can we pay, and what happens after that?" Work out a runway:

  1. Monthly income your parent has: Social Security, pensions, annuities.
  2. Savings and investments that can be drawn down.
  3. The house: will it be sold, rented, or kept for a spouse?
  4. Long-term care insurance, if there is a policy, and its daily benefit and elimination period.
  5. Veterans benefits: a wartime veteran or surviving spouse may qualify for VA pension with Aid and Attendance.
  6. Family contributions, and whether they are sustainable for years.

Divide the total available by the realistic monthly cost, including the care level your parent will need, and you have the number of months the money lasts. If that number is short, plan for it now. Ask every community whether it accepts residents on TennCare CHOICES, and what happens to a resident whose money runs out. Some Memphis-area communities do; many do not.

Three of our guides go deeper: what assisted living costs and what the rate includes, how families pay, and what happens when the money runs out.

4. Fit: the community your parent will actually live in

Only once the first three are settled does fit decide anything. By now your list should be short: communities that are licensed, can meet today's care needs, have the right kind of unit, and cost something the family can sustain.

Fit is real and it matters. A parent who is miserable will decline faster. Fit includes:

  • Location. Close enough that family can visit often. In Memphis that usually means thinking about which side of town: Germantown, Collierville, East Memphis and Cordova have most of the larger communities; Midtown, Bartlett and Arlington have fewer. Families in Southaven, Olive Branch, Horn Lake and Hernando often look across the state line, and families in West Memphis and Marion often look east over the bridge.
  • Size. A large community with a hundred or more apartments has more activities and more staff on site. A small one with a dozen residents feels like a house and the staff know everyone well.
  • The residents. Is your parent going to find people they can talk to? Look at the residents during a tour, not only the staff.
  • Food. Eat a meal there. Three meals a day is a large part of what your parent will experience.
  • Faith and culture. Several Memphis communities have a church or faith tradition behind them; for some parents that matters a great deal.
  • Doctor and hospital. Is it convenient for your parent's physician and the hospital they use?

Before you tour: check the licence

Every assisted living community in Tennessee must hold a licence from the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission. The directory on each city page lists every licensed community in Shelby County with its licence number, phone number and whether it has secured memory care beds, taken from the Commission's own published list.

Check two things for each community on your short list:

  • The licence is current, and the type matches what you need.
  • The most recent inspection, called a survey, and how any deficiencies were corrected.

Our guide to reading a Tennessee inspection record explains where to find it and what is normal.

How to run the search in two weeks

Most families do not have months. A hospital discharge, a fall or a carer's illness forces the decision in days or weeks. This order works when time is short.

  1. Day 1 to 2: write down care needs and memory, get the medication list from the doctor, and list the money available.
  2. Day 2 to 3: from the directory, list every licensed community within the distance family can travel. Mark the ones with memory care if you need it.
  3. Day 3 to 5: phone each one. Ask three questions: do you have an opening in the right type of unit, can you meet these care needs, and what is the all-in monthly price at that care level? Cross off anyone who says no to the first two.
  4. Day 5 to 10: tour the three that remain. Use the same tour checklist at each so you compare like with like. Go back unannounced to the one you prefer, at a mealtime or early evening.
  5. Day 10 to 14: request the residency agreement from your first choice, read it, and ask about anything unclear before you sign. Our residency agreement guide covers what to look for.

If your parent is in hospital, start with the hospital's discharge planner. Our guide to moving from hospital to assisted living covers what they can do for you and what you need ready.

Questions to ask every community

  • Can you meet my parent's care needs today? What would make you say you could not?
  • What care level would you place my parent at, and what is the monthly price at that level, all in?
  • What happens to the price, and to my parent's place, if their needs increase?
  • Do you have a secured memory care unit? How many beds, and is one open?
  • How many care staff are on duty during the day and overnight, and is a nurse on site?
  • When did the state last inspect you, and can I see the report?
  • Do you accept TennCare CHOICES? What happens if a resident's private funds run out?
  • How much notice do you require, and in what circumstances can you ask a resident to leave?

Signs to slow down

  • A community that will not give a price until after an assessment, and will not even give a range.
  • Pressure to sign the same day, or a "special" that ends this week.
  • A licence that does not match what is promised, such as memory care offered by a community with no secured beds on its licence.
  • Vague answers about overnight staffing.
  • Reluctance to let you see the most recent inspection or to visit unannounced.
  • A residency agreement you are not allowed to take away and read.

Involving your parent

Where your parent can take part in the decision, they should. People who choose where they live settle better than people who are moved. Even a parent with moderate dementia can usually tell you which of two dining rooms they prefer.

That does not mean your parent must agree before anything happens. If they are not safe at home and refuse to consider any move, our guide on when a parent refuses to move covers how families actually get through that conversation.

If you are not sure assisted living is the right level

Assisted living is not the only option, and sometimes it is the wrong one. Independent living suits a parent who is lonely or tired of maintaining a house but needs little hands-on help. A nursing home suits a parent who needs a nurse every day. Home care can work for a parent who needs a few hours of help and has family nearby. Our guide to levels of care in Tennessee sets them side by side, with what the state licenses each one as.

faq.q: What is the most important factor in choosing a senior care home?
faq.a: Care needs come first. A community that cannot meet your parent's needs today, or will not be able to as they grow, is the wrong choice however good it looks. Settle care needs, memory and money before you judge fit.

faq.q: How many licensed assisted living communities are there in Shelby County?
faq.a: The Tennessee Health Facilities Commission's July 2026 bed report lists 31 licensed Assisted Care Living Facilities in Shelby County, 23 of which report secured memory care beds. Each city page on this site lists them with licence numbers and phone numbers.

faq.q: How long does it take to find a care home in Memphis?
faq.a: Families under time pressure can usually narrow the list, tour and choose within about two weeks if they settle care needs and budget first. Admission then depends on an open apartment, the community's assessment and the paperwork, which can take a few more days.

faq.q: Should I choose a large or a small community?
faq.a: Large communities have more staff on site and more activities; small residences feel more like a home and staff know each resident well. The right size depends on your parent's personality and needs. The care they need matters more than the size.

faq.q: Can my parent move from assisted living to memory care in the same community?
faq.a: Only if the community has a secured unit. Twenty-three of the 31 licensed communities in Shelby County do. If dementia is part of the picture, choosing one with a secured unit avoids a second move later.

faq.q: Does it cost anything to use this guide?
faq.a: No. Families never pay us. Senior living communities pay us a referral fee or a flat fee when they accept a family we introduce, and some buy sponsored placements, which are labelled. The directory lists every licensed community regardless.

faq.q: What if my parent is in hospital now?
faq.a: Ask for the hospital's discharge planner or case manager straight away and tell them you are looking at assisted living. They can share the discharge summary and orders communities need, and help you avoid a discharge home that is not safe.

faq.q: Should my parent tour before deciding?
faq.a: Yes, wherever they can. People who take part in choosing where they live tend to settle better. If your parent cannot tour, bring photos and a menu home, and ask them which feels right.
